domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: A patient aspirates gastric contents and becomes hypoxic. What is the mainstay of therapy?
answer: Positive-pressure ventilation; intubation + PEEP or NIV as needed.
rationale: Hypoxia from aspiration results from alveolar flooding and shunting; PPV recruits alveoli and maintains oxygenation.

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: After confirmed aspiration of particulate matter in the OR, what procedure is indicated beyond PPV?
answer: Bronchoscopy and pulmonary lavage.
rationale: Solid particles obstruct airways and cannot be cleared by PPV alone; bronchoscopic removal prevents ongoing obstruction and infection.

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: Should prophylactic antibiotics be given immediately after witnessed aspiration?
answer: No; antibiotics are given only based on culture results, not empirically at the time of aspiration.
rationale: Early antibiotic prophylaxis does not improve outcomes in aspiration pneumonitis and may select resistant organisms.
confusable_with: aspiration pneumonia (established infection requiring targeted antibiotics)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: In a high-aspiration-risk obstetric patient, what pre-induction pharmacologic measures reduce aspiration severity?
answer: Metoclopramide, H2-blockers, and non-particulate antacids.
rationale: These agents reduce gastric volume, raise gastric pH, and accelerate emptying, limiting lung injury if aspiration occurs.
confusable_with: proton pump inhibitors (slower onset, less useful acutely)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What is the recommended maximum bag-mask ventilation pressure to minimise aspiration risk?
answer: Keep airway pressure below 20 cmH2O during bag-mask ventilation.
rationale: Pressures >20 cmH2O open the lower oesophageal sphincter and force gas into the stomach, increasing regurgitation risk.

enabling_conditions: Full stomach, impaired airway reflexes, obesity, pregnancy, GERD, emergency or unplanned intubation
pathophysiology: Gastric contents flood alveoli causing chemical pneumonitis (acid) or mechanical obstruction (particulate); increased alveolar-capillary permeability leads to hypoxic respiratory failure
time_course: Hypoxia within minutes; pneumonitis peaks 4-6 h; bacterial superinfection in 24-72 h if particulate
key_features: Witnessed regurgitation or sudden hypoxia/bronchospasm; wheezing, crackles; CXR infiltrates in dependent lobes
consequence_if_missed: Progression to ARDS, bacterial pneumonia, respiratory failure, death

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: A patient has necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis, upper/lower respiratory tract granulomas, and glomerulonephritis. Which ANCA pattern and antigen is most characteristic?
answer: c-ANCA pattern, anti-PR3 antibody (granulomatosis with polyangiitis).
rationale: GPA is predominantly anti-PR3 positive, producing the cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) immunofluorescence pattern because PR3 is distributed throughout the neutrophil cytoplasm.

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: Approximately what proportion of microscopic polyangiitis patients are anti-MPO positive vs anti-PR3 vs ANCA-negative?
answer: ~70% anti-MPO positive, ~20% anti-PR3, ~10% ANCA-negative.
rationale: MPA predominantly triggers MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) because myeloperoxidase is the primary antigenic target in MPA pathogenesis.

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: Why can the diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis not rely on serology alone?
answer: Positive ANCA occurs in other conditions (SLE, infective endocarditis, chronic hepatitis); clinical and histologic correlation is required.
rationale: ANCA lacks 100% specificity; tissue biopsy remains the gold standard for confirming vasculitis.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA Wegener)

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: In double-positive antibody disease (ANCA + anti-GBM), what organ patterns predominate?
answer: Renal disease follows anti-GBM pattern; systemic symptoms resemble ANCA vasculitis.
rationale: Positive ANCA precedes anti-GBM (ANCA exposes GBM epitopes); treatment must address both pathways, typically including plasmapheresis.

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: Which drug class is a recognised trigger for drug-induced ANCA vasculitis?
answer: Anti-TNF-alpha agents (for RA/ankylosing spondylitis); also hydralazine and propylthiouracil.
rationale: These drugs can induce ANCA production by altering neutrophil antigen expression or inducing neutrophil extracellular traps.

discriminator: GPA: granulomas + upper respiratory (saddle-nose, sinusitis) + anti-PR3/c-ANCA. MPA: no granulomas + predominantly anti-MPO/p-ANCA; both cause RPGN.

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What intervention is associated with the greatest improvement in ARDS mortality of any RCT-tested treatment?
answer: Reduced tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight — ARDSnet strategy).
rationale: Low tidal volume limits volutrauma and barotrauma; this is the single intervention with the strongest mortality benefit in ARDS RCTs.
confusable_with: High PEEP strategy (benefit less certain on mortality)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: The Berlin definition classifies ARDS by PaO2/FiO2 ratio. What are the thresholds for mild, moderate, and severe?
answer: Mild: PaO2/FiO2 201-300; moderate: 101-200; severe: <=100 mmHg.
rationale: The 2012 Berlin definition uses these P/F cutoffs to stratify severity and guide management intensity.
confusable_with: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (P/F may overlap but PCWP <18 in ARDS)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What plateau pressure limit is targeted in lung-protective ventilation for ARDS?
answer: Plateau pressure <30 cmH2O.
rationale: Plateau pressure reflects alveolar distending pressure; keeping it below 30 cmH2O reduces barotrauma and ventilator-induced lung injury.
confusable_with: Peak airway pressure (includes resistance component; higher and less specific)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What is the fundamental pathophysiologic distinction between cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
answer: Cardiogenic = elevated hydrostatic pressure; non-cardiogenic (ARDS) = increased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability.
rationale: The distinction guides therapy: cardiogenic responds to diuresis/afterload reduction; ARDS requires lung-protective ventilation targeting the permeability defect.

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: At what FiO2 and duration does oxygen toxicity become a clinical concern in mechanically ventilated patients?
answer: 100% O2 for up to 10-20 hours is generally safe; FiO2 >50-60% is undesirable for prolonged periods.
rationale: Alveolar O2 tension drives toxicity via reactive oxygen species; minimising FiO2 prevents superimposed oxygen toxicity in ARDS patients.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Name the three mechanisms of ventilator-associated lung injury that lung-protective ventilation targets.
answer: Barotrauma (excess pressure), volutrauma (excess volume), and atelectrauma (cyclic alveolar opening/closing).
rationale: Low tidal volumes limit volutrauma and barotrauma; adequate PEEP prevents atelectrauma by maintaining alveolar recruitment throughout the respiratory cycle.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Why is permissive hypercapnia accepted in ARDS management?
answer: Allowing PaCO2 to rise is accepted to achieve low tidal volume (6 mL/kg IBW) and limited plateau pressures (<30 cmH2O).
rationale: Reducing tidal volume reduces CO2 elimination; the trade-off of mild respiratory acidosis is tolerated because lung-protective ventilation dramatically reduces mortality.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: A ventilated patient suddenly develops increased peak airway pressure AND increased plateau pressure simultaneously, with arterial hypotension. What must be immediately excluded?
answer: Tension pneumothorax.
rationale: Simultaneous rise in peak and plateau pressures with haemodynamic collapse indicates high intrathoracic pressure impairing venous return — tension pneumothorax.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: On spirometry, restrictive pulmonary disease shows what pattern?
answer: Reduced FEV1 and FVC with preserved (normal or elevated) FEV1/FVC ratio; total lung capacity reduced.
rationale: Decreased lung compliance reduces all volumes proportionally; expiratory flow is preserved, distinguishing restriction from obstruction.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: In damage control surgery for abdominal trauma, what two immediate goals take priority over definitive repair?
answer: Stop haemorrhage AND limit GI contamination; definitive repair is deferred to a planned relook.
rationale: DCS prioritises physiologic stabilisation over anatomic repair to break the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Which artery is most commonly injured in pelvic trauma and where does it exit the pelvis?
answer: Superior gluteal artery (branch of internal iliac); exits at the sciatic notch.
rationale: The superior gluteal artery is the largest branch of the internal iliac and is vulnerable at the sciatic notch in pelvic ring fractures.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What does a FAST exam identify and what is its key limitation in pelvic trauma?
answer: Identifies free fluid (blood/peritoneal fluid) but cannot differentiate blood from bowel contents and cannot assess retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
rationale: FAST detects free fluid by ultrasound but lacks specificity for its nature; CT is required for full characterisation in haemodynamically stable patients.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Which point-of-care coagulation tests allow targeted resuscitation in pelvic haemorrhage?
answer: Thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM).
rationale: TEG/ROTEM assess clot formation, strength, and fibrinolysis in real time, guiding goal-directed transfusion of FFP, platelets, and cryoprecipitate.
confusable_with: Standard coagulation tests (INR/aPTT — slower and less actionable)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What is added to IV resuscitation fluids in paediatric burn patients <30 kg that differs from adult protocols?
answer: 5% dextrose is added to IV fluids.
rationale: Children have higher glucose turnover and limited glycogen stores; they are prone to hypoglycaemia during major fluid resuscitation.
confusable_with: Adult burn resuscitation (Parkland formula without dextrose)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What is the current recommended adult maximum daily dose of acetaminophen?
answer: 3000 mg/day (reduced from 4000 mg/day).
rationale: Hepatotoxicity risk approaching 4 g/day led to downward revision; the margin is further reduced with alcoholism, malnutrition, or enzyme-inducing drugs.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Which substances potentiate acetaminophen hepatotoxicity?
answer: Isoniazid, zidovudine, barbiturates, and chronic alcohol use.
rationale: These agents induce CYP2E1, increasing production of toxic NAPQI metabolite; alcohol and malnutrition also deplete hepatic glutathione reserves.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Acute liver failure from acetaminophen is defined by what two criteria?
answer: Severe acute liver injury with impaired synthetic function (INR >=1.5) PLUS altered mental status, occurring without pre-existing liver disease.
rationale: The two-criterion definition (coagulopathy + encephalopathy) distinguishes acute liver failure from compensated liver injury and drives transplant evaluation.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: In an obtunded patient with unknown ingestion, what empiric IV triad is given while awaiting toxicology?
answer: Naloxone (up to 2 mg), dextrose 50% (50 mL), and thiamine (100 mg) IV.
rationale: This triad treats the three most reversible causes of coma: opioid overdose, hypoglycaemia, and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

enabling_conditions: Intentional overdose; chronic excess dosing especially with alcohol or enzyme inducers; unintentional multi-source exposure
pathophysiology: NAPQI metabolite saturates glutathione; binds hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular necrosis; renal tubular injury may occur
time_course: Phase 1 (0-24h): nausea/vomiting; Phase 2 (24-72h): RUQ pain, transaminase rise; Phase 3 (72-96h): peak hepatotoxicity, possible ALF; Phase 4: recovery or transplant
key_features: RUQ pain, jaundice, rapidly rising ALT/AST (>10,000 IU/L possible), coagulopathy, encephalopathy in ALF
consequence_if_missed: Irreversible ALF requiring liver transplant; death from cerebral oedema or multi-organ failure

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: By KDIGO criteria, what urine output threshold and duration defines AKI?
answer: Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for at least 6 hours.
rationale: KDIGO uses both creatinine and urine output criteria; the patient is staged by whichever gives the highest (worst) stage.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What is the prevalence of AKI among ICU admissions?
answer: Approximately 30% of ICU admissions develop AKI.
rationale: ICU patients have multiple concurrent risk factors (sepsis, nephrotoxins, haemodynamic instability) making AKI the most common renal problem in critical care.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: Which agents cause pre-renal AKI through renal vasoconstriction?
answer: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors, and hepatorenal syndrome.
rationale: These reduce intraglomerular pressure by constricting afferent arterioles or reducing systemic perfusion, dropping GFR without tubular injury.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: Which drugs raise serum creatinine without reducing GFR?
answer: Trimethoprim (Bactrim), cimetidine (H2-blocker), and dronedarone — they block tubular creatinine secretion.
rationale: Creatinine is both filtered and secreted; drugs blocking tubular secretion raise serum Cr while BUN remains stable, mimicking AKI without GFR decline.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: In hepatorenal syndrome type 1, what is the initial terlipressin dose and escalation strategy?
answer: Terlipressin 1 mg IV every 6 hours; escalate to 2 mg every 6 hours at 48-72 hours if creatinine reduction <20-30%.
rationale: Terlipressin is a V1-receptor vasopressin analogue that increases splanchnic vasoconstriction and improves renal perfusion pressure in HRS.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: When calculating the anion gap in metabolic acidosis, what adjustment is required for accuracy?
answer: Correct for albumin: add 2.5 mEq/L per 1 g/dL fall in albumin below 4 g/dL.
rationale: Albumin is the major unmeasured anion; hypoalbuminaemia lowers the apparent normal anion gap, masking a true high-AG acidosis if uncorrected.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Metabolic Acidosis  Approach and Anion Gap

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What is the maximum safe rate of peripheral IV potassium replacement?
answer: No more than 8 mEq/hr peripherally; central venous administration needed for 10-20 mEq/hr (with continuous ECG monitoring).
rationale: High local potassium concentration causes chemical phlebitis in peripheral veins; rapid central replacement risks arrhythmia.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: In a digoxin-treated patient requiring potassium repletion, what K+ target should be maintained?
answer: Plasma K+ > 4 mEq/L.
rationale: Hypokalaemia sensitises the myocardium to digoxin toxicity by competing with K+ at the Na+/K+-ATPase; higher K+ levels are protective.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: Why should dextrose-containing IV solutions be avoided during potassium replacement for hypokalaemia?
answer: Dextrose causes hyperglycaemia -> insulin release -> intracellular K+ shift -> worsens hypokalaemia.
rationale: Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, driving K+ into cells; glucose-containing fluids create a counter-productive cycle during K+ replacement.

domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What is the first step in AKI management regarding the medication list?
answer: Hold nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs); avoid contrast if possible; chase contrast with fluids if unavoidable.
rationale: Removing the ongoing insult is the first step; ACEi/ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure and worsen pre-renal AKI.

topic: Acute Pancreatitis & GI Emergencies in ICU
domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What physical exam findings suggest haemorrhagic pancreatitis with retroperitoneal bleeding?
answer: Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) and Grey-Turner sign (flank ecchymosis).
rationale: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracks along fascial planes to the umbilical region and flanks, indicating severe necrotising or haemorrhagic pancreatitis.

topic: Acute Pancreatitis & GI Emergencies in ICU
domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What two radiographic signs on abdominal plain film suggest acute pancreatitis?
answer: Sentinel loop (localised ileus of adjacent bowel) and colon cutoff sign (abrupt gas termination at splenic flexure).
rationale: Both reflect localised peritoneal inflammation causing adynamic ileus adjacent to the pancreas; non-specific but suggestive.

topic: Acute Pancreatitis & GI Emergencies in ICU
domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: Using the CT Severity Index (CTSI), what score range indicates severe acute pancreatitis?
answer: CTSI score 8-10 (out of 10).
rationale: The CTSI adds points for pancreatic necrosis and peripancreatic collections; high scores correlate with complications, ICU admission, and mortality.

topic: Acute Pancreatitis & GI Emergencies in ICU
domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: What pulmonary complication is visible on CXR in severe acute pancreatitis?
answer: Pleural effusions and ARDS infiltrates.
rationale: Systemic inflammation from pancreatic injury increases alveolar-capillary permeability; ARDS can develop in severe/necrotising cases.

topic: Acute Pancreatitis & GI Emergencies in ICU
domain: Internal medicine: ICU & critical care (all-cause shock, vasopressors & inotropes, invasive & noninvasive ventilation, sedation & analgesia, multiorgan failure, rapid response, ACLS)
stem: After alcohol-related acute pancreatitis, what fraction of patients progress to chronic pancreatitis?
answer: Approximately one-third after a single episode; recurrence and progression risk are elevated without abstinence.
rationale: Ongoing alcohol exposure perpetuates acinar cell injury and fibrosis; abstinence is the key modifiable preventive factor.

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: Anterior cord syndrome spares which sensory modalities and why?
answer: Proprioception, vibratory sense, and fine touch are preserved because the dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries (not the anterior spinal artery).
rationale: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord; the dorsal columns carrying proprioception/vibration are perfused by the paired posterior spinal arteries.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Acute Spinal Cord Injury & Syndromes

confusable_with: Central cord syndrome (arms > legs weakness, variable sensation)

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What is the most common cause of anterior spinal artery syndrome?
answer: Aortic surgery (most common); also aortic dissection, hypotensive shock, AVMs.
rationale: The anterior spinal artery receives contributions from radiculomedullary arteries jeopardised during aortic cross-clamping or dissection.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Acute Spinal Cord Injury & Syndromes

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: Why are autonomic symptoms absent in some anterior cord syndrome cases?
answer: Lateral horns (sympathetic preganglionic neurons) exist only between T1 and L2; ischaemia outside this region spares autonomic function.
rationale: Sympathetic outflow originates in the T1-L2 lateral horn neurons; injury at cervical or lower lumbar levels does not directly disrupt this segment.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Acute Spinal Cord Injury & Syndromes

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: How is neurogenic hypotension in high cervical spinal cord injury managed?
answer: IV fluids and vasopressors to maintain MAP.
rationale: Loss of sympathetic outflow causes vasodilation and bradycardia (neurogenic shock); vasopressors restore vascular tone.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Acute Spinal Cord Injury & Syndromes

confusable_with: Haemorrhagic shock (expected tachycardia; neurogenic shock has bradycardia)

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What is the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosing anterior spinal artery syndrome?
answer: MRI of the spine.
rationale: MRI demonstrates signal changes in the anterior cord; DWI sequences show restricted diffusion in acute ischaemia with superior soft-tissue resolution.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Acute Spinal Cord Injury & Syndromes

enabling_conditions: Aortic surgery, aortic dissection, hypotensive shock, spinal AVM, percutaneous spinal procedures
pathophysiology: Occlusion of anterior spinal artery -> ischaemia of anterior 2/3 of cord -> motor paralysis + spinothalamic loss; dorsal columns (proprioception/vibration) spared
time_course: Acute onset; late sequelae include spasticity, neurogenic bladder, sexual dysfunction
key_features: Acute back pain at injury level; bilateral motor paralysis; loss of pain/temperature bilaterally; preserved proprioception/vibration
consequence_if_missed: Permanent paralysis; no acute-specific treatment; management is supportive (MAP optimisation, DVT/pressure-sore prophylaxis)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: How does angioedema differ from urticaria clinically?
answer: Urticaria: superficial dermal pruritic wheals. Angioedema: deep subcutaneous/submucosal nonpitting oedema, not usually pruritic, may threaten the airway.
rationale: Urticaria involves superficial dermal mast cell mediator release; angioedema involves deeper tissues and can compromise the larynx/tongue.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Why does bradykinin-mediated angioedema not respond to epinephrine or antihistamines?
answer: Because it is kinin-mediated (bradykinin increases permeability/vasodilation), not IgE/histamine-mediated.
rationale: Epinephrine and antihistamines target the IgE/mast-cell axis; bradykinin-mediated angioedema (HAE, ACEi-induced) requires kinin pathway-targeted therapy.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What specific agents treat ACEi-induced bradykinin-mediated angioedema?
answer: C1 inhibitor replacement protein (C1INHRP) or fresh frozen plasma (FFP).
rationale: ACEi prevents bradykinin degradation; treatment requires interrupting the bradykinin pathway rather than the histamine/IgE axis.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Angioedema at which anatomical level causes upper airway vs lower airway obstruction?
answer: Pharynx/larynx/trachea -> upper airway obstruction; bronchospasm + mucosal oedema -> lower airway obstruction.
rationale: Laryngeal involvement is immediately life-threatening; bronchospasm/mucosal oedema produce wheezing and hypoxia from lower airway obstruction.

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: Activation of Hageman factor (factor XII) during severe angioedema can initiate what additional dangerous process?
answer: Intravascular coagulation (DIC).
rationale: Hageman factor activates the contact/intrinsic coagulation pathway; massive mast-cell/kinin activation can trigger systemic coagulation cascade.
